topic: How an online order reaches a customer's door: order, pick and pack, hub sort, delivery route, and where delays happen
scope_note: Generic, process-level chain (retailer or third-party warehouse, then a parcel network). No numbers, no named retailers or carriers. Details vary by company; the five-station model is a teaching simplification.

facts.statement: An online order passes through a chain of separate stages, each handing the parcel or the order data to the next, rather than being one continuous event.
facts.reference_hint: Standard order-to-delivery / order fulfilment descriptions in logistics and supply chain textbooks

facts.statement: The five stations used in this lesson are order, pick, pack, hub sort and delivery route; real companies may split or merge these steps.
facts.caveat: A teaching simplification. Real networks add steps such as receiving at a depot, or a returns loop. Say it as 'the way we will look at it'.

facts.statement: When an order is placed, the retailer's system checks payment, usually by asking the card issuer to authorise the amount, which reserves the funds rather than moving them at once.
facts.caveat: Usually, not always: some businesses capture payment immediately or at dispatch. Keep wording to 'checks or authorises payment'.
facts.reference_hint: Card payment authorisation versus capture, as described in payment processor documentation

facts.statement: Many retailers also run fraud checks and address checks on a new order, and an order that fails or is flagged can be held until it is resolved.
facts.caveat: Not every retailer does each check, and the checks differ in depth.

facts.statement: The order system allocates stock to the order and then releases it to a warehouse, where it appears as work to be picked.
facts.reference_hint: Order management and warehouse management system descriptions in fulfilment literature

facts.statement: Retailers set order cut-off times: an order placed before the cut-off can be handled in the current dispatch cycle, and one placed after it usually waits for the next.
facts.caveat: The actual cut-off time differs by retailer, product and delivery option, so the script must not give a clock time.

facts.statement: Stock shown as available on a website can turn out not to exist in the warehouse, because the inventory records and the physical shelves can disagree.
facts.reference_hint: Inventory record accuracy, a standard topic in warehouse and inventory management texts

facts.statement: Picking means collecting the ordered items from their storage locations, guided by a pick list or a scanner instruction.
facts.reference_hint: Order picking, standard warehouse operations term

facts.statement: Warehouses reduce walking by grouping orders into batches or waves, or by bringing the goods to the picker (goods-to-person) instead of sending the picker to the goods.
facts.caveat: Methods vary by site; many small warehouses simply pick order by order.
facts.reference_hint: Order picking methods (batch, wave, goods-to-person) in warehouse management texts

facts.statement: At the packing station the items are checked, often by scanning, put in a box or bag, and a shipping label is printed and attached.
facts.caveat: The scan-to-verify step is common but not universal.

facts.statement: Common failure points in the warehouse are a wrong item picked, an item not found at its recorded location, stock found to be missing at pick time, and a backlog when order volume peaks.
facts.reference_hint: Typical order picking error and capacity issues in warehouse operations literature

facts.statement: A hub is a central sorting site where parcels from many origins are scanned and sorted by destination, such as postcode or route, onto outbound vehicles.
facts.reference_hint: Hub-and-spoke network model in transport and parcel logistics texts

facts.statement: In a hub-and-spoke network, parcels travel from the origin to a hub, then on to a hub or depot near the destination, instead of going directly between every pair of places.
Linehaul is the long-distance trunk movement between hubs and depots, and parcel networks often run it overnight.
facts.caveat: Often overnight, not always; timing differs by network and distance.

facts.statement: Because linehaul trucks leave on a schedule, a parcel that misses its departure usually waits for the next one.
facts.caveat: Depends on the network's departure frequency; say 'usually waits for the next departure'.

facts.statement: Hub sorting can go wrong when a label is damaged or unreadable so the scanner cannot route the parcel, or when a parcel is sorted onto the wrong route.
facts.reference_hint: Parcel sortation process descriptions in logistics literature

facts.statement: At the local depot, parcels are loaded onto vans, usually in the order of the planned route, and the driver delivers along that route.
facts.caveat: Route planning is often done by software; load order often follows the planned stops but practices vary.

facts.statement: A delivery attempt ends in proof of delivery, such as a signature, a photo or a scan, recorded at the door.
facts.caveat: The form of proof depends on the carrier and service.

facts.statement: Typical last-mile problems are nobody home or no access at the first attempt, a wrong or incomplete address, a van with too little room, and weather or traffic.
facts.reference_hint: Last-mile delivery challenges, common in logistics literature

facts.statement: The last mile, the final leg to the customer, is commonly described as the most expensive and least efficient part of the delivery chain per parcel.
facts.caveat: Widely repeated, but exact shares vary by study and market, so give no figure and say 'commonly described as'.
facts.reference_hint: Capgemini Research Institute, The Last-Mile Delivery Challenge (2019), and logistics textbooks; the wording here is not verified against the report

facts.statement: Each tracking status in a parcel's history is normally created by a scan or data event at a hand-off point, not by continuous live location of the parcel.
facts.caveat: Some carriers show live van position only in the final stretch; most of the journey shows scan events. Do not say tracking is live GPS.
facts.reference_hint: Carrier tracking help pages on scan events

facts.statement: Typical status meanings: order confirmed means the retailer accepted the order; dispatched means it has left the warehouse; in transit or at hub means it is moving through the network; out for delivery means it is on the van for its route; delivered means proof of delivery was recorded; delivery attempted means the driver tried and did not complete it.
facts.caveat: Wording differs between carriers and retailers; explain the meaning, not exact labels.

facts.statement: A long gap between two scans can mean the parcel is waiting at a station, such as a hub or depot, so the last status names the place to look.
facts.caveat: An inference from how scan tracking works: a gap can also be a missed scan while the parcel moves normally, so say 'often points to'.

terms.definition: collecting items from storage locations for an order
a central site where parcels are sorted by destination
long-distance trunk transport between hubs and depots
the final leg from the local depot to the customer's door
the time before which an order is handled in the current dispatch cycle
the point where the order or parcel passes from one stage to the next, usually recorded by a scan

not_claimed: Tracking is live GPS for the whole journey
Any specific percentage, hours or days for any station
A specific cut-off clock time that applies everywhere
Any statistic on how often orders are late or which station causes most delays
The last mile accounts for a specific share of cost
Delays are caused by careless individual workers
Any real retailer or carrier fails more than others
Every retailer runs identical checks and stations
